newsitem.title: DENMARK: FOCUS-Danish central bank generally bullish for 97.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Danish central bank generally bullish for 97.

text.p: Denmark's central bank said on Thursday the country's economic prospects for 1997 were bright but it called for continued fiscal restraint in 1998 to keep wages and prices under control.
"The outlook for the Danish economy in 1997 is in many respects brighter than it has been for a long time," the National Bank said in its 1996 annual report.
It said that the present economic upturn was expected to gather momentum, the current account indicated a surplus and the public sector budget was seen coming out of deficit in 1997.

But it added that although price and wage rises were for the time being moderate, they should be kept under close control and the report urged the government to maintain in 1998 its tight fiscal stance -- 0.5 percent of GDP in 1997.

"The current account surplus is of a such a modest amount that it could quickly disappear. With a continued significant level of foreign debt it is essential that the current account surplus is preserved at least at its present level," it said.

"In light of the presumption that 1997 will be the fourth consecutive year with good economic growth and that the public sector budget is expected to balance in 1997, there is a need for a tightening of public finances in 1998," it added.
"The main goal of economic policy during the coming year is to control domestic demand to ensure low rises in pay and prices and a continued balance of payments surplus," it said.

Full-year 1996 data showed a current account surplus of 10.9 billion crowns, compared to 9.4 billion in 1995, but monthly figures show the balance going from a 0.2 billion surplus in October 1996 to a 6.6 billion deficit in November and a 2.3 billion shortfall in December.
Detailing the central bank's own accounts the report said that it ended 1996 with a surplus of 5.867 billion crowns, compared to 4.805 billion the year before.
It said that it put 1.092 billion crowns into its new currency regulation fund, and 1.432 billion into its contingency fund, transferring the remaining 3.342 billion to state coffers.
It added that net foreign exchange reserves rose 21 billion crowns in 1996 to 85 billion.
